# Problem 1
##### The goal is to do some exploration of this dataset. To that end, write a short description of the dataset, noting the size and structure of the data, describing some key variables, and indicating the extent to which missing data is an issue. 
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")
```

The NY NOAA dataset include weather data from all New York state weather stations from January 1, 1981 through December 31, 2020, from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association. The dataset include `r nrow(ny_noaa)` daily weather observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables. Two of the variables serve as identifiers, including a character identifier for the weather station and a date for each daily weather observation at that station. Weather measurements include precipitation (tenths of millimeters), snowfall (millimeters), snow depth (millimeters), maximum temperature (tenths of degrees Celsius), and minimum temperature (tenths of degrees Celsius). While the dataset is tidy in structure, there is extensive missingness among the measurement variables, as each weather station may not have collected all five measurements. Of the `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations, missingness occurred for `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp)))` precipitation measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow)))` snowfall measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snwd)))` snow depth measurements, `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax)))` maximum temperature measurements, and `r sum(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmin)))` minimum temperature measurements. 

##### Do some data cleaning. Create separate variables for year, month, and day. Ensure observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall are given in reasonable units. For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?
```{r}
ny_noaa_clean = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(!is.na(prcp) | !is.na(snow) | !is.na(snwd) | !is.na(tmax) | !is.na(tmin)) |> 
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10, 
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
    ) |> 
  relocate(id, date, year, month, day, everything()) 

ny_noaa_clean |> 
  group_by(snow) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(count))
```

Data cleaning first involved removing any observations in which all five weather measurements were missing. Next, I generated the year, month, and day for each measurement date. Finally, the minimum and maximum temperatures were stored as character type, which I converted to numeric type. Furthermore, the minimum and maximum temperatures were stored in unintuitive units, tenths of degrees Celsius, such that I divided by ten so that the units would be degrees Celsius; I did the same for precipitation which was stored as tenths of millimeters.  

The most commonly observed values for snowfall, other than missing, were 0 millimeters (n=2008508), 25 millimeters (n=31022), and 13 millimeters (n=23095). Those measurements correspond to approximately 0, 1, and 0.5 inches, respectively, which makes sense as to why they are the most commonly observed.

##### Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers? 
```{r, message = FALSE}
ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7,
         !is.na(tmax)) |> 
  group_by(id, month, year) |> 
  summarize(tmax_avg = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    month = case_when(
      month == 1 ~ "January",
      month == 7 ~ "July")
    ) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(x = year, y = tmax_avg, group = year)) + 
  facet_grid(~month) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Average Maximum Temperature in January and July by Year", 
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (Celsius)"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, 5))
```

This boxplot illustrates the distribution of average maximum temperature in January or July by year across weather stations. There are a few interesting observations. First, the median average temperature is more variable over time in January than July. Second, the distribution of average temperature in January appears to be shifting to warmer temperatures over time, while the distribution in July does not appear to be changing over time. Finally, whereas the outliers in July are exclusively lower-tail outliers, the outliers in January are lower- and upper-tail outliers. 

##### Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.
```{r}
tmax_tmin = ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmin) | !is.na(tmax)) |> 
  select(tmin, tmax) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    tmin:tmax, 
    names_to = "measurement",
    names_prefix = "t",
    values_to = "temperature"
    ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(temperature)) |> 
  mutate(
    measurement = case_when(
      measurement == "min" ~ "Minimum \n Temperature",
      measurement == "max" ~ "Maximum \n Temperature")
    ) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(y = measurement, x = temperature)) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Minimum and Maximum Temperature", 
    x = "Temperature (Celsius)",
    y = "Measurement"
    )

snowfall = ny_noaa_clean |> 
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarize(number_of_snowfalls = n()) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_col(mapping = aes(x = year, y = number_of_snowfalls)) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfalls Greater than 0 Millimeters and Less than 100 Millimeters", 
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Snowfalls"
    ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2010, 5))

tmax_tmin / snowfall
```

This two-panel plot illustrates the (1) distribution of minimum and maximum temperature across the entire dataset, and (2) distribution of snowfalls greater than 0 millimeters and less than 100 millimeters. For the temperature boxplot, the distribution of minimum temperature was lower than maximum temperature, and there are lower- and upper-tail outliers for both minimum and maximum temperature. For the snowfalls histogram, the number of snowfalls greater than 0 millimeters and less than 100 millimeters was stable around 5000 per year from 1980 to 2006 but, since 2006, increased rapidly, exceeding 10000 in 2010. 

# Problem 2

##### Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables; exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data; and encode data with reasonable variable classes (i.e. not numeric, and using factors with the ordering of tables and plots in mind).
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes_covar <- read_csv("Data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_when(
      sex == 1 ~ "Male",
      sex == 2 ~ "Female"
      ),
    education = case_when(
      education == 1 ~ "Less than High School",
      education == 2 ~ "High School Equivalent",
      education == 3 ~ "More than High School"
      ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(education, levels = c("Less than High School", 
                                             "High School Equivalent",
                                             "More than High School"))
    ) |> 
  filter(age >= 21, 
         !is.na(bmi),
         !is.na(education)
    )

nhanes_accel <- read_csv("Data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
    ) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes <- inner_join(nhanes_accel, nhanes_covar, by = "seqn") |> 
  relocate(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education)
```

The clean and tidy dataset from the NHANES study combines demographic and accelerometer data for `r length(unique(pull(nhanes, seqn)))` participants. Demographic variables include sex (male, female), age (years), body mass index, and education level (less than high school, high school equivalent, more than high school). The accelerometer data are the Monitor-Independent Movement Summary unit (MIMS) in each minute of a 24-hour day beginning at 12:00am. The `r length(unique(pull(nhanes, seqn)))` participants have `r nrow(nhanes)` MIMS observations. An important step in data cleaning included removing participants younger than 21 or for whom demographic data was missing; only body mass index and education level had missingness among demographic variables. 

##### Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes |> 
  select(seqn, sex, education) |> 
  unique() |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sex", "Education Level", "Count"))

nhanes |> 
  select(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  unique() |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_boxplot(mapping = aes(x = age, y = sex)) + 
  facet_wrap(~education) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Sex",
    title = "Distribution of Age by Sex and Education Level"
    )
```

These exhibits provide the number of participants and their age distribution by sex and education level. Among males, 27 completed less than high school, 35 completed high school or an equivalent, and 56 completed more than high school. Among females, 28 completed less than high school, 23 completed high school or an equivalent, and 59 completed more than high school. Therefore, the most common education was completing more than high school among males and females, comprising approximately one-half of participants of each sex, with the other two education levels comprising approximately one-fourth of participants of each sex. The boxplot visualizes the distribution of age by sex and education. For participants completing less than high school or more than high school, the distribution of age by sex was similar. In contrast, for participants completing high school or an equivalent, the distribution of age was lower for males than females.

##### Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.
```{r, message = FALSE}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  summarize(mims_total = sum(mims)) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = age, y = mims_total, color = sex)) + 
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = age, y = mims_total, color = sex), se = FALSE) + 
  facet_wrap(~education) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Activity Over the Day (MIMS)",
    title = "Total Activity Over the Day by Sex and Education Level"
    ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank()
    )
```

This exhibit illustrates the total activity over the day of participants by sex and education level. For each sex and education level, there is a downward trend for total activity with greater age, which is expected considering the effects of aging on mobility. The trajectory of the downward trend varies considerably by sex and education level. For example, the trend is most consistently negative for participants who completed less than high school. Furthermore, the downward trends do not monotonically decrease, with, for example, total activity markedly increasing before eventually decreasing for participants who completed high school or an equivalent, especially among females. 

##### Accelerometer data allows the inspection activity over the course of the day. Make a three-panel plot that shows the 24-hour activity time courses for each education level and use color to indicate sex. Describe in words any patterns or conclusions you can make based on this graph; including smooth trends may help identify differences.
```{r, message = FALSE, fig.width = 12}
nhanes |> 
  mutate(hours = (minute - 1)/60) |> 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = hours, y = mims, color = sex), size = 0.11, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_smooth(mapping = aes(x = hours, y = mims, color = sex), se = FALSE) + 
  facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Hour of the Day \n(0 is 12:00am, 1 is 1:00am, ..., 23 is 11:00pm)",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    title = "Activity by Sex and Education Level"
    ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.box.spacing = unit(0, "pt"),
    plot.title = element_text(margin = margin(t = 5, b = -2, unit = "pt"))
    ) + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 23, 1),
    expand = c(0, 0)
    ) + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 40))
```

This exhibit illustrates 24-hour activity time courses by sex and education level. While the activity data are by minute, the x-axis was labeled by hour, as hour of the day was thought to be more interpretable than minute of the day. One other important design consideration was trunctating the y-axis to between 0 and 40 to improve readability. Although the smooth curves were generated using all data, 310 activity observations had MIMS greater than 40 and are not pictured. 

There are a couple of interesting observations. First, the 24-hour activity time course is similar by sex and education, peaking during daytime versus bottoming out during nighttime. Second, there appears to be slight differences in 24-hour activity course between males and females within each education level, and those differences vary among education levels as well. For example, among participants completing less than high school, males tend to be more active at night and in the early morning, with males and females being similar the rest of the day. In contrast, among participants completing more than high school, males and females are similar at night and in the early morning, but females are more active the rest of the day. 

# Problem 3
##### Files contain 1% of all rides with a total duration less than 4 hours in each of four months. Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset.
```{r, message = FALSE}
citi_jan_2020 <- read_csv("Data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month_year = "January, 2020") |> 
  relocate(month_year, ride_id, rideable_type)
citi_jan_2024 <- read_csv("Data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month_year = "January, 2024") |> 
  relocate(month_year, ride_id, rideable_type)
citi_july_2020 <- read_csv("Data/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month_year = "July, 2020") |> 
  relocate(month_year, ride_id, rideable_type)
citi_july_2024 <- read_csv("Data/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(month_year = "July, 2024") |> 
  relocate(month_year, ride_id, rideable_type)

citi <- bind_rows(citi_jan_2020, citi_jan_2024, citi_july_2020, citi_july_2024) |> 
  mutate(
    member_casual = case_when(
      member_casual == "member" ~ "Citi Bike Member",
      member_casual == "casual" ~ "Casual Rider"
      ),
    rideable_type = case_when(
      rideable_type == "classic_bike" ~ "Classic Bike",
      rideable_type == "electric_bike" ~ "Electric Bike"
      )
    ) |> 
  rename(
    bike_type = rideable_type, 
    day_of_week = weekdays, 
    rider_type = member_casual
    ) 
```

The clean and tidy dataset includes 1% of all rides with a total duration less than 4 hours in January 2020, January 2024, July 2020, and July 2024. Each ride is identified by a string of numbers and letters and by its month and year pairing. Additional information include the rider type (Citi Bike member, casual rider), bike type (classic bike, electric bike), day of the week, duration (minutes), start station name, and end station name. The dataset include `r nrow(citi)` rides. 

##### Produce a reader-friendly table showing the total number of rides in each combination of year and month separating casual riders and Citi Bike members. Comment on these results.
```{r, message = FALSE}
citi |> 
  group_by(month_year, rider_type) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = rider_type,
    values_from = count
    ) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Month, Year", "Casual Rider", "Citi Bike Member"))
```

This exhibit shows the total number of rides for casual riders and Citi Bike members in January 2020, January 2024, July 2020, and July 2024. In each month and year pairing, ridership is more common among Citi Bike members than casual riders. Furthermore, for each rider type, in both 2020 and 2024, ridership is more common in July than January. Finally, for each rider type, in both January and July, ridership is more common in 2024 than 2020. 

##### Make a table showing the 5 most popular starting stations for July 2024; include the number of rides originating from these stations.
```{r, message = FALSE}
citi |> 
  filter(month_year == "July, 2024") |> 
  group_by(start_station_name) |> 
  summarize(count = n()) |> 
  arrange(desc(count)) |> 
  slice_max(count, n = 5) |> 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Starting Station", "Number of Originating Rides"))
```

This exhibit features the 5 most popular starting stations for rides in July 2024, all of which are in Manhattan! 

##### Make a plot to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. This plot can include one or more panels, but should facilitate comparison across all variables of interest. Comment on your observations from this plot.
```{r, message = FALSE}
citi |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_when(
      month_year == "January, 2020" ~ "January",
      month_year == "January, 2024" ~ "January",
      month_year == "July, 2020" ~ "July",
      month_year == "July, 2024" ~ "July"
      ),
    year = case_when(
      month_year == "January, 2020" ~ "2020",
      month_year == "January, 2024" ~ "2024",
      month_year == "July, 2020" ~ "2020",
      month_year == "July, 2024" ~ "2024"
      ),
    day_of_week= factor(day_of_week, 
                      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", 
                                 "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")
                      )
    ) |>
  group_by(year, month, day_of_week) |> 
  summarize(duration_median = median(duration)) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_col(mapping = aes(x = day_of_week, y = duration_median, fill = year), position = "dodge") + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Day of the Week in January and July, 2020 versus 2024"
    ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank()
    ) 
```

This exhibit illustrates the relationship between median ride duration and day of the week, month, or year. There are a few interesting observations. First, median ride duration is bimodal across days of the week. Specifically, median ride duration is similar between Monday and Friday--the weekdays--and is similar on Saturday and Sunday--the weekend. Second, irrespective of day of the week or year, median ride duration is longer in July than January. Finally, irrespective of day of the week and month, median ride duration is shorter in 2024 than 2020. Altogether, this exhibit suggests median ride duration may have consistent day of the week and seasonal patterns while becoming shorter over time. 

##### There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.
```{r}
casual = citi |> 
  filter(month_year == "January, 2024" | month_year == "July, 2024",
         rider_type == "Casual Rider") |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_when(
      month_year == "January, 2024" ~ "January",
      month_year == "July, 2024" ~ "July"
      )
    ) |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_density(mapping = aes(x = duration, fill = month), alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ bike_type) + 
   theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Duration",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of Ride Duration by Month and Bike Type for Casual Riders in 2024"
    ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_blank()
    ) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.00, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08), 
                     limits = c(0.00, 0.08)
                     )

member = citi |> 
  filter(month_year == "January, 2024" | month_year == "July, 2024",
         rider_type == "Citi Bike Member") |> 
  mutate(
    month = case_when(
      month_year == "January, 2024" ~ "January",
      month_year == "July, 2024" ~ "July"
      )
    ) |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_density(mapping = aes(x = duration, fill = month), alpha = 0.5) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ bike_type) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(
    x = "Duration",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of Ride Duration by Month and Bike Type for Citi Bike Members in 2024"
    ) + 
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_blank()
    ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.00, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08))

casual / member
```

These exhibits illustrate the relationship between the distribution of ride duration and month, bike type, or membership status. The top panel describes the distribution of ride duration by month and bike type for casual riders. For both classic and electric bikes, the distribution of ride duration is more concentrated among shorter rides in January than July. Furthermore, in both January and July, the distribution of ride duration is more concentrated among shorter rides for electric bikes than classic bikes. 

Next, the bottom panel describes the distribution of ride duration by month and bike type for Citi Bike members. For classic bikes, but not electric bikes, the distribution of ride duration is similar in January and July. For electric bikes, the distribution is more concentrated among shorter rides in January than July. Furthermore, the distribution of ride duration is more concentrated among shorter rides in January for electric bikes than classic bikes, whereas the distribution is more concentrated among shorter rides in July for classic bikes than electric bikes.
